---
title: "From tidy data to models"
---

## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
```

## Two kinds of questions

When we want to predict something,
the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

- Regression, when the outcome is *quantitative*.
  What will this house sell for?
  How heavy will this baby be at birth?
- Classification, when the outcome is *categorical*.
  Will this patient's cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we'll fit a linear regression.
On Wednesday we'll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

## Models need tidy data

A model formula like `price ~ sqft` expects the data to have
one row per observation (each house sale)
and one column per variable (the price and the size),
which is what tidy data gives us.

## Sacramento house sales

These are house sales in Sacramento, California,
from the modeldata package that comes with tidymodels.

```{r}
Sacramento
```

## Is size related to price?

```{r}
ggplot(Sacramento, aes(x = sqft, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "House size (square feet)", y = "Sale price (USD)")
```

## Linear regression: the line of best fit

$$
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
$$

- $\beta_0$ is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
- $\beta_1$ is the slope,
  how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The "best" line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances
between the line and the data points.

## Fit it with tidymodels

```{r}
house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)
house_fit
```

## Read the coefficients

```{r}
tidy(house_fit)
```

For every extra square foot,
the predicted price goes up by about `r round(tidy(house_fit)$estimate[2])` USD.

## See the line

```{r}
ggplot(Sacramento, aes(x = sqft, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "House size (square feet)", y = "Sale price (USD)")
```

## More than one predictor

$$
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_m X_m
$$

To use more predictors, we add them to the formula.

```{r}
recipe(price ~ sqft + beds + baths, data = Sacramento)
```

Now each slope is how much the outcome changes for one predictor,
when the other predictors stay the same.
